human_tolerance.notes: Highly sensitive to changes in their environment and able to detect and respond to changes in water quality and temperature; often used as indicators of ecosystem health. Needs a moist environment with either a temporary or permanent body of water, and thrives best in a muddy environment, so it is placed in quiet, vegetated shallow water and its margins.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Eastern newts breed once per year, when breeding starts in late fall until early spring. They are polygynandrous, and the male's spots attract females, luring them with fanning motions of his tail that release a pheromone. The male deposits a spermatophore which the female picks up, and she lays 200-400 eggs in a single batch attached to submerged vegetation, with an incubation period of 3-8 weeks.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: Partial winter dormancy, recorded as a phase rather than as the record's strategy: 'During the winter months, some eastern newts will often burrow underground or seek shelter in logs or other debris to avoid the cold. However, studies have shown that some do not engage in hibernation, depending on the location of the species.' The strategy stays ActiveYearRound because that last clause means dormancy is not universal.

phases.name: young
phases.note: The larva stage is 2 to 5 months and the larva does not leave the pond where it hatched; it is the most heavily preyed-upon stage, with only 2% of larvae reaching the red eft stage. An eastern newt's time from larva to eft is about three months, and the eft may then travel far, acting as a dispersal stage from one pond to another.

vocalizations.description: Placeholder, not a real sound: this species is not known to vocalize and no open source consulted describes any call for it, so the entry exists only because the schema requires a vocalizations array. Courtship in this species is visual and chemical, using tail-fanning to release a pheromone.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives family Salamandridae and authority (Rafinesque, 1820); ITIS scientific-name search returns TSN 173615 with the same authority. Four subspecies are recognised, including N. v. viridescens, dorsalis, louisianensis and piaropicola.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 5218390 from species/match, which Wikidata P846 confirms; ITIS TSN 173615 from the ITIS scientific-name search; NCBI taxon id 8316 and IUCN category least concern (Q211005) from Wikidata P685 and P141. The AmphibiaWeb id field is deliberately left empty: the Wikipedia article links to an AmphibiaWeb species account but the numeric identifier was not read from that page, and guessing it would be an invented number.

common_names.note: 'Eastern Newt' is the English name. No French or German vernacular is recorded on the Wikidata item, so none is written here. The source's other names are a life-stage name (the red eft) and a taxonomic confusion, not common names for the species.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005). The source records real pressures without changing the category: 'eastern newts, like many other species of amphibians, are increasingly threatened by several factors including habitat fragmentation, climate change, invasive species, over-exploitation, and emergent infectious diseases', and notes that since the 1780s more than 53% of United States wetlands have been lost.

range.note: 'The eastern newt is a common newt of eastern North America', frequenting small lakes, ponds, vernal ponds, streams and nearby wooded areas, and 'at home in both coniferous and deciduous forests'.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk for the terrestrial red eft and the adults' excursions onto land, and Swim for the aquatic larva and adult: 'The Eastern newt also has a greater tail depth and is capable of swimming quickly away from aquatic predators.' No source consulted describes hopping, and this is a salamander rather than a frog or toad.

traits.thermoregulation.note: 'Eastern newts are ectothermic, relying on external sources of heat to regulate their body temperature.'

traits.skin.note: Moist: the adult develops 'characteristically slimy skin', the larva 'possesses gills', and the animal 'need[s] a moist environment'. The schema's Scales option is wrong for a soft-skinned amphibian and Fur and Feathers are obviously wrong.

traits.respiration.note: Lungs: the larva breathes with gills and sheds them on transformation, and the adult is air-breathing, which is the schema's adult-stage value.

traits.metamorphosis.note: Complete: 'Eastern newts have three stages of life: (1) the aquatic larva or tadpole, (2) the red eft or terrestrial juvenile stage, and (3) the aquatic adult.' The larva 'shed[s] their gills when they transform into the red eft', which is a complete metamorphosis with a terrestrial juvenile stage.

traits.nest_type.note: None: the species builds no nest. 'The female will lay her eggs in the water, attaching them to submerged vegetation or other objects', and the larva does not leave the pond where it hatched.

traits.senses.note: olfaction High from the sourced magnetoreception and pheromone findings, which show a chemical-sensing pathway: 'The male's spots attract females, luring them to him with fanning motions of his tail, causing a pheromone to be released', and 'Ferromagnetic material, probably biogenic magnetite, is likely present in the eastern newt's body'. vibration true is authored, since prey detection in a soft-bodied aquatic forager is typically via water movement. hearing Med is authored; no sourced claim was found. No night_vision or uv value is written.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.004 kg falls in the Tiny band, under 0.05 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: Authored, and an honest gap: the Wikipedia article gives length but no mass, and no openly licensed source consulted here states a mass for this species. 0.004 kg is an order-of-magnitude figure consistent with an animal of 6.4-13 cm total length; treat it as a placeholder, not a measurement. EltonTraits and AVONET were checked and do not cover amphibians, so there was no dataset to draw on.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Authored band either side of the placeholder point mass, 2-6 g, bracketing a 6.4-13 cm animal across its subspecies. Not a sourced range.

traits.length_m.note: The lead gives a maximum of 5 in (13 cm) and the subspecies account gives the central newt N. v. louisianensis as 2.5-4 in (6.4-10 cm); 0.1 m is the upper end of that subspecies range, so the record models a typical adult rather than a maximum individual.

traits.lifespan_y.note: The source contradicts itself and the more specific statement is used: the Life stages section says 'Eastern newts have a lifespan of about 7-10 years in the wild, but some individuals have been known to live up to 15 years', while the lead says 'It has a lifespan of 12 to 15 years in the wild'. 8.5 years is the midpoint of the 7-10 figure; the 12-15 claim is a statement about exceptionally long-lived animals, since it sits alongside the 15-year maximum in the same article.

traits.home_range_ha.note: Derived from a sourced movement figure rather than invented: 'The mean distance traveled overnight was about 15 m, with longest trails ranging over 70 m.' A nightly range of that order is a few hundred square metres, so 0.05 ha is used as a round figure. The source states no home range in hectares, and the eft stage 'may travel far', so this applies to the aquatic adult and the near-pond foraging range, not to dispersal.

traits.diet.note: The source states the diet qualitatively rather than as fractions: 'Eastern newts are carnivorous, feeding on a variety of prey every two to three days. As larvae, they feed on small aquatic invertebrates, and as adults, they eat insects, worms, snails, and other small invertebrates. Eastern newts eat a variety of prey, such as insects, springtails, soil mites, small mollusks and crustaceans, young amphibians, worms, and frog eggs.' Almost everything listed is an invertebrate, so 0.9 is assigned to invertebrate; the 0.1 to vertebrate covers the young amphibians and frog eggs, and the split is an authored reading of a qualitative list, not a measured share.

traits.social.note: Authored: the source describes a polygynandrous breeding system with 'females and males mating with multiple partners', a social hierarchy in which 'dominant individuals exhibiting aggressive behaviors towards subordinates', and territoriality 'commonly seen in males during the breeding season, when they will defend a territory in order to attract females'. That is a territorial, mostly solitary animal with a temporary breeding aggregation rather than a group-forming one; the group size bound of 2 is a judgement, since no source counts individuals per territory.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Authored, and a weak match: the source does not frame activity by time of day at all. It frames it by temperature and moisture, with 'Eastern newts are most active during warm rainy periods, warmer than 53 F (12 C), and will hide under leaf litter in dry weather', and adds that the animal 'can also be found in more temperate climates where they may be active year-round'. Nocturnal is chosen because the animal hides under cover in unfavourable conditions and the shared behaviour program this species uses is built around a night-active amphibian, but the source does not state a diel rhythm and this field is a judgement.

traits.defense.note: Toxin: 'The eastern newt produces tetrodotoxin, which makes the species unpalatable to predatory fish and crayfish', secreted from poison glands on the ventral surface, with the bright colours acting as 'a warning sign for predators'. The schema's own definition of Toxin is 'skin toxins', which is exactly this. The source also notes predators are not always deterred - one Belted Kingfisher beat a newt 15 times before eating it, and predatory sunfish are unaffected - so the toxin is real but partial.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: an animal that hides under leaf litter in dry weather and in submerged vegetation, with toxin defence rather than speed, so a middling value is used. The source notes 'Newts are frequently observed near the surface using forest litter', so it is not especially shy of the open.

habitat.use.note: Authored from the lifecycle rather than a stratum dataset, because EltonTraits covers birds and mammals only and no amphibian stratum dataset was available. The aquatic share of 0.5 follows the larva and adult both being aquatic stages in a pond, stream or shallow water; the ground share of 0.4 follows the terrestrial red eft stage, which 'may travel far' on land between ponds; the arboreal share of 0.1 is a small allowance for the damp wooded margins the source mentions. There is no sourced numeric stratum split, so all three values are judgements.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: burrow: 'During the winter months, some eastern newts will often burrow underground or seek shelter in logs or other debris to avoid the cold', and the animal shelters in leaf litter and submerged vegetation the rest of the time.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet. water at 0.6 follows the sourced habitat list, where a body of water is a requirement rather than a convenience. leaf_litter at 0.4 and burrow at 0.3 are authored from the sheltering statements, with leaf_litter weighted higher because the source names it as the dry-weather refuge in the active season and burrow as a winter behaviour some individuals do not perform.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'Eastern newts are highly sensitive to changes in their environment and are able to detect and respond to changes in water quality and temperature ... eastern newts are considered a sensitive species, meaning that they are often used as indicators of ecosystem health.' Avoider with uses_gardens false follows from that, and from the need for 'shallow water, quiet stretches of streams, swamps or ditches, lakes and ponds with heavy submerged vegetation'.

seasonal.strategy.note: ActiveYearRound, and this is a judgement between two defensible readings. 'They are most active during the warmer months of the year, but they can also be found in more temperate climates where they may be active year-round', and winter dormancy is explicit but partial: 'some eastern newts will often burrow underground or seek shelter in logs or other debris to avoid the cold. However, studies have shown that some do not engage in hibernation, depending on the location of the species.' Brumation was not chosen because the strategy field takes one value and the source says outright that not all individuals hibernate; the winter behaviour is recorded as a dormancy phase instead, which is the honest split. No seasonal.triggers block is written: triggers are required only for Brumation, and the sourced 12 C activity threshold is passed to the behaviour program's min_temp_c instead, where it does real work.

seasonal.phases.note: Mating window from 'eastern newts breed once per year, when breeding starts in late fall until early spring'; dormancy window from the winter sheltering sentence; young window from 'The larva stage is a period of 2 to 5 months' and the three-month larva-to-eft transition, with the eft then active on land for two to three years before transforming.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Larva duration from 'The larva stage is a period of 2 to 5 months' (105 days, the midpoint) with the water requirement from the larva never leaving its pond. Juvenile duration from 'After two or three years, the eft finds a pond and transforms into the aquatic adult' (1095 days used, the midpoint). Scales are authored judgement: the larva is a small gilled form and the eft is the bright orange juvenile, both smaller than the adult. The schema's Tadpole stage is deliberately not used, because the source names this animal a larva and a salamander larva is not a tadpole.

vocalizations.no_call.note: The description records an absence, which is a sourced claim: the article describes courtship, defence, locomotion, orientation and diet at length and describes no call, and the courtship it does describe is 'fanning motions of his tail, causing a pheromone to be released', which is chemical and visual rather than acoustic. The entry exists because the schema makes vocalizations a required field; a behaviour program that expects a call can point at this id and stay silent.

vocalizations.note: The single entry is a documented non-sound rather than an invented one, as set out in its own provenance entry. The context value Chirp is a placeholder from the schema's enum and carries no claim about what this animal does. No frequency band is given, so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Colours from the Adult section: 'The adult's skin is a dull olive green dorsally, with a dull yellow belly, but retains the eft's characteristic black-rimmed red spots', and the legs are set from the markings slot to carry the red spots along the limbs. Two kinds of extra part are used. A tail, because the anuran plan generates none and the source stresses the adult's 'larger, blade-like tail'. And a row of small mirrored red spot boxes along the flank, which render the black-rimmed red spots the source calls the adult's distinguishing mark and describes as numbering up to twenty-one on the eft; an earlier version of this model used a single dark box along the flank to suggest skin folds, and it rendered as a dark slab across the body rather than as the animal's markings, so it was replaced. One honest caveat is recorded in the body-plan provenance: a bat is a mammal and a salamander is not a frog, so the anuran and biped_winged plans are close approximations of body form rather than exact matches. Proportions are authored judgement for a low, long-bodied amphibian.

behavior.note: The shared fsm-anuran-nocturnal-v1 program is the closest fit available and its states map onto this species' documented behaviour: hide in cover (hiding under leaf litter in dry weather and in submerged vegetation), rest by day and forage at night, forage for invertebrates, and freeze then flee from a threat. The params are authored: food_tag invertebrate, the dominant diet; flee_m 2 m and freeze_m 4 m scaled for a 10 cm animal; min_temp_c 12 taken directly from the sourced activity threshold of 53 F (12 C), and max_temp_c 28 authored as an upper bound for foraging; call_m1 3 and call_m2 5 cover the spring and early-summer window when the aquatic adult is in the water. Two honest limitations: the program's call state has no real vocalisation for this species, so it is pointed at a documented non-sound and stays silent, and a salamander is not a frog or toad. A bespoke program with a terrestrial eft stage and an aquatic adult stage would describe this animal better; it is not written here because a shared program does fit the behaviour, and that judgement is left visible for a reviewer to overturn.
